claims.text: A thin CVD-deposited SiC coating on zirconium-alloy cladding will improve resistance to high-temperature oxidation.
The SiC coating will preserve the cladding's mechanical integrity for service.
The proposed SiC coating should be approximately 1–2 μm thick, dense, and adherent.
Chemical vapor deposition can produce the proposed SiC coating on zirconium-alloy cladding.
Exposure to steam at approximately 1200°C simulates severe-accident conditions for zirconium-alloy cladding.
The intervention will form a continuous SiC layer that adheres well to the cladding surface.
SiC has chemical inertness and thermal stability relevant to high-temperature steam exposure.
The SiC layer will act as an oxidation barrier by reducing oxygen ingress into the zirconium substrate.
Reduced oxygen ingress will lower the oxidation rate relative to uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding.
The coating will mitigate rapid oxide growth during high-temperature steam exposure.
At approximately 1200°C in steam, coated cladding will show significantly lower mass gain than uncoated cladding.
At approximately 1200°C in steam, coated cladding will develop a thinner oxide layer than uncoated cladding.
The coated cladding will retain the mechanical properties required for service.
The coated cladding will retain the neutronic properties required for service.
The beneficial effect depends on the coating being uniform, defect-free, and within an optimal thickness range.
Poor coating quality or unsuitable thickness can cause defects or spallation and adversely affect performance.
The magnitude of oxidation-rate reduction depends on coating microstructure, thickness uniformity, and adhesion.
